strengths: The paper targets an underexplored but meaningful vision problem: separating cast and attached shadows rather than treating all shadows as a single class. This is well motivated by physical differences between projected shadows and self-shadowing, and the work is relevant to scene understanding, lighting estimation, compositing, and shadow removal.

The dataset contribution is potentially valuable. The paper curates 1,458 images from WSRD, SOBA, and CUHK with separate cast, attached, undefined-shadow masks, estimated normals, and heuristic light directions. Even if imperfect, this appears to be one of the first benchmarks enabling quantitative attached-shadow evaluation.

The method has a plausible physics-grounded design: surface normals and an estimated light direction generate a partial attached-shadow prior, which is fed back into a multi-class shadow detector. The iterative shadow-light loop is conceptually clean and connects classical illumination reasoning with modern segmentation models.

Results show a clear improvement for attached-shadow detection. On the proposed test set, attached-shadow BER improves substantially over SBU-pretrained and retrained baselines, and attached F1 reaches 86.49 versus 80.72 for the strongest retrained baseline. Ablations support the importance of normal guidance, iterative refinement, and light-related losses.

The paper includes useful qualitative examples and a limitations section that honestly discusses dependence on normal-map quality, lack of cast-attached instance association, and the single directional-light assumption.
weaknesses: The main contribution type is closer to a dataset/benchmark plus applied system than a purely algorithmic paper. Under that framing, the dataset is important, but the paper does not provide enough evidence about annotation quality: no inter-annotator agreement, ambiguity analysis, quality-control protocol, or statistics on attached/cast/undefined regions are reported in the main paper.

The evaluation protocol raises fairness concerns. Prior shadow detectors produce a single shadow mask and are split into cast/attached using object masks, whereas the proposed method is trained for explicit multi-class prediction with normals and light priors. Several baselines are retrained only with full-shadow supervision rather than with the same cast/attached labels, so the comparison partly measures task supervision mismatch rather than only method quality.

The benchmark is partly circular: object masks are used for annotation/evaluation, normals come from an off-the-shelf depth/normal estimator, and light directions for SOBA/CUHK are heuristic estimates derived from object-shadow centroids and relative depth. These derived signals may encode biases that favor the proposed geometry-based model, but the paper does not quantify their errors or robustness.

The light-estimation module is central to the claimed closed-loop reasoning, yet there is no direct quantitative evaluation of light-direction accuracy or of how errors in light estimation affect segmentation. The light targets are heuristic for much of the dataset, making it unclear whether the model learns real illumination or dataset-specific proxy cues.

Generalization evidence is limited. All quantitative results are on the newly curated dataset, with no cross-dataset evaluation, no tests on indoor/night/multi-light scenes, and no robustness study for normal-map degradation. This matters because the method assumes a single directional light and relies strongly on generated geometry.

The algorithmic novelty is moderate. The architecture combines known segmentation backbones, off-the-shelf normals, a simple dot-product attached-shadow prior, and iterative refinement. The strongest scientific contribution is the problem/dataset framing rather than a substantially new learning method.

Performance gains are not uniformly strong: full-shadow BER is essentially tied with retrained SILT, cast-shadow BER is worse than SILT, and the iterative version triples inference time relative to the non-iterative baseline. The main empirical benefit is concentrated in attached-shadow metrics on the authors' own benchmark.

strengths: The paper identifies a real and underexplored problem: separating attached shadows from cast shadows, rather than treating all shadows as a single foreground class. This is a meaningful direction for shadow understanding and downstream geometry/illumination reasoning.

The proposed dataset, if released with clear annotation protocol and splits, could be useful because it provides separate cast/attached/undefined masks over 1,458 images curated from existing shadow datasets.

The method incorporates plausible physical cues through surface normals and an estimated directional light, and the ablations suggest that normals, iterative feedback, and the light-related losses each improve attached-shadow metrics.

The experimental tables show substantial gains in attached-shadow BER/F1 over retrained full-shadow baselines on the proposed test set, while maintaining competitive full-shadow and cast-shadow performance.
weaknesses: The central technical contribution is quite limited. The physics module is essentially a dot product between off-the-shelf normals and a single estimated light direction, followed by iterative feedback into a segmentation network adapted from prior work. The formulation is intuitive but not especially novel or deeply developed.

The dataset and supervision are a major concern. The paper restricts fine-grained annotation to foreground objects and labels other shadows as undefined, so the benchmark is only partially annotated. This weakens claims of detecting cast and attached shadows across full natural scenes, and Fig. 6 even evaluates qualitative predictions outside the labeled regions without ground truth.

The light-direction labels for most data are heuristic, derived from object/shadow centroids and relative depth estimated from monocular cues. This creates noisy pseudo-ground truth, yet the light estimator is trained and regularized against it. The paper does not quantify the accuracy of these light labels or evaluate light estimation independently.

The evaluation against prior methods is not fully convincing. Baselines are retrained only with full-shadow supervision rather than with the same cast/attached labels and comparable multi-class outputs, while their predictions are split using object masks at evaluation time. This makes it hard to isolate whether the gain comes from the proposed physics loop, access to class-specific supervision, normal maps, or evaluation protocol differences.

There is no cross-dataset or external generalization experiment. Since training and testing are on the newly curated dataset with its own annotation rules and heuristic labels, the reported gains may not transfer to unconstrained scenes or different definitions of attached shadows.

The assumptions are restrictive: a single scene-wide directional light, monocular off-the-shelf normals, foreground-object-centric annotations, and no explicit cast/attached instance association. These limitations directly affect the claimed physics grounding and applicability to indoor, night-time, multi-object, or multi-light scenes.

Important implementation and reproducibility details are deferred to supplementary material: architectural modifications, annotation details, data quality checks, inter-annotator agreement, and exact processing pipelines are not sufficiently specified in the main paper.

The paper’s claims feel stronger than the evidence supports. In particular, calling the method physics-grounded overstates a simple approximate cue that ignores visibility, interreflection, non-Lambertian materials, multiple lights, and occlusion geometry, all of which are central to attached-shadow formation.

strengths: The paper addresses a real and underexplored gap in shadow understanding: separate detection of cast and attached shadows. The motivation is convincing, since attached shadows carry geometry and illumination information but are largely collapsed into generic shadow masks in existing datasets and methods.

The proposed contribution is appropriately framed as an applied/systems contribution combining dataset construction, a geometry-aware model, and iterative light-shadow refinement. It does not merely chase a benchmark number; it creates a task formulation and benchmark that could be useful for future work on scene understanding, relighting, compositing, and shadow removal.

The method is technically plausible and well motivated. Using estimated normals and a directional-light estimate to derive a partial attached-shadow prior is a simple but effective way to inject physical structure into a modern segmentation system. The iterative loop between shadow detection and light estimation is intuitive and supported by ablations.

The empirical results are strong on the proposed benchmark, especially for attached shadows. The reported attached-shadow BER improves substantially over both SBU-pretrained and dataset-retrained baselines, and the F1 improvements are consistent. The ablation table supports the value of normals, iterative refinement, and the light-related losses.

The new dataset with separate cast, attached, and undefined shadow masks is a meaningful resource. The paper is transparent that annotations are foreground-object focused and that undefined regions are excluded from cast/attached evaluation, which is an important practical design choice rather than a hidden flaw.

The paper is clearly written overall, with helpful qualitative figures, dataset examples, and a limitations section that identifies important constraints such as normal-map dependence, lack of instance-level cast/attached association, and single directional-light assumptions.
weaknesses: The dataset is relatively small at 1,458 images, and the annotation protocol limits fine-grained cast/attached labels mainly to foreground objects. This is reasonable for an initial benchmark, but it also means the results may not fully establish generalization to dense real-world scenes with many objects, complex geometry, and multiple shadow interactions.

The light-direction supervision is partly heuristic for SOBA and CUHK, derived from object-to-cast-shadow displacement and relative depth. This may introduce systematic noise, yet the paper does not provide a strong validation of light-direction accuracy or quantify how errors in these pseudo-labels affect the iterative loop.

The comparison to prior methods is useful but not completely definitive. Several baselines are retrained only for full-shadow supervision and then split using object masks, whereas the proposed method is trained directly with cast/attached labels and uses normals/light priors. Stronger controls, such as a same-backbone multi-class detector without physics, parameter/FLOP-matched variants, and baselines trained with the same cast/attached supervision, would better isolate the contribution of the physical feedback mechanism.

The physical model is simplified. The method assumes a single scene-wide directional light and uses a local normal-dot-light test for attached-shadow priors, without modeling visibility, interreflection, material effects, or multiple light sources. The authors acknowledge some of this, but the claims about physics-grounding should be interpreted within this limited model.

Some formulation details would benefit from more precision. The sign convention in the attached-shadow rule depends on how normals and the light vector are oriented, and the text should make this unambiguous. Additional details on normal generation, undefined-mask handling during training/evaluation, iterative unrolling, and whether code/data will be released are needed for reproducibility.

The method increases inference cost roughly linearly with iteration count, and the paper reports a 3x slowdown for the chosen setting. This is acceptable for many applications, but the practical tradeoff between accuracy and runtime could be discussed more fully, especially since five iterations do not consistently improve class-specific metrics.

strengths: Addresses a meaningful and underexplored vision problem: explicitly separating cast and attached shadows rather than treating shadows as a single binary mask. The motivation is clear and relevant to downstream tasks such as shadow removal and scene/light understanding.

The paper contributes both an algorithmic framework and a curated benchmark with separate cast/attached/undefined annotations, which could be useful for future work even if the dataset is modest in size.

The proposed light-geometry feedback loop is intuitive and reasonably grounded in image formation: surface normals plus an estimated dominant light direction provide a plausible prior for attached shadows.

Quantitative results on the proposed dataset show large gains for attached-shadow detection, especially relative to retrained binary shadow detectors, and the ablations support the importance of normals, iterative refinement, and light-related losses.
The paper is generally clear, includes useful qualitative examples, reports computational overhead, discusses limitations, and provides supplementary details on annotation and architecture.
weaknesses: The main experimental comparison is not fully convincing. Several baselines are retrained only with full-shadow binary supervision, while the proposed method receives cast/attached labels, normals, and pseudo light-direction supervision. This makes the reported attached-shadow gains partly a comparison of supervision and inputs rather than architecture alone. Stronger baselines adapted to multi-class cast/attached segmentation with the same normal inputs are needed.

The dataset construction has potential circularity: attached masks for SOBA are initialized from the same derived light direction and normal maps that the method later uses, then manually corrected. This may bias the benchmark toward the proposed physical prior unless annotation independence and correction quality are more rigorously validated.

The cast/attached evaluation protocol depends on object masks and excludes undefined regions. Since annotations are foreground-object centered, the benchmark may under-measure full-scene ambiguity and overstate performance on clean object-associated shadows. The claim that the model predicts coherent full-image labels outside annotated regions is only qualitative.

The light-estimation supervision is weak for most of the dataset: SOBA/CUHK light directions are heuristic pseudo-labels from object-shadow centroids and estimated depth, and quantitative light evaluation is only on 42 WSRD test images. This limits the strength of claims about accurate light reasoning.

Cross-dataset generalization and the shadow-removal application are mostly qualitative or based on a small preference study without quantitative ground truth. These support plausibility but not strong external validation.

The method relies on off-the-shelf monocular depth/normal estimates and a single dominant directional light assumption, which limits applicability to indoor, multi-light, soft-shadow, nighttime, or geometrically complex scenes. The paper acknowledges this, but the experiments do not quantify the failure envelope.

strengths: The paper addresses a real gap: most shadow-detection work treats shadows as a single mask, while explicit cast/attached separation is useful for physical scene understanding and downstream editing tasks.
The proposed dataset is potentially valuable, since it provides separate cast, attached, and undefined shadow labels over 1,458 images curated from WSRD, SOBA, and CUHK.

The method has a plausible physical motivation: attached shadows depend on surface orientation and illumination, and the iterative loop between shadow prediction and light estimation is conceptually coherent.

The main quantitative table shows large gains for attached-shadow detection over several retrained baselines, and the ablations indicate that normals, light-related losses, and iterative feedback each contribute to performance.
The paper includes limitations, runtime analysis, some light-estimation diagnostics, and a small downstream shadow-removal user study, which help clarify intended use and practical tradeoffs.
weaknesses: The experimental case is not fully convincing because the dataset construction, supervision, and evaluation are tightly coupled to the same geometry/light assumptions used by the proposed method. Attached masks for SOBA are initialized from derived light directions and normal maps before manual correction, so there is a risk of circularity favoring the proposed geometry-based approach.

The light-direction annotations for most images are heuristic rather than ground truth, derived from object-shadow centroids and estimated relative depth. This weakens the physical claims, especially because light estimation is a central module and is quantitatively validated only on 42 WSRD test images.

The comparison to prior methods is not entirely fair for the cast/attached task. Many baselines are binary shadow detectors retrained with full-shadow supervision and then split using object masks, whereas the proposed method is trained with explicit cast/attached labels. Stronger baselines would include multiclass adaptations of the same architectures trained with the same labels, and variants using the same normal/depth inputs without the proposed iterative light loop.

The evaluation protocol excludes undefined regions for cast/attached metrics and uses object masks in evaluation, while annotations cover mainly foreground objects. This makes the benchmark less representative of full-scene cast/attached separation and may inflate apparent performance relative to real deployment.

The generalization evidence is mostly qualitative. Cross-dataset results on SRD, SBU-TimeLapse, and ViSha do not provide quantitative cast/attached evaluation, so the claim of robustness beyond the curated dataset remains weak.

The physical model is quite simplified: a single dominant directional light, approximate normals from monocular depth, and a local dot-product attached-shadow rule without visibility or interreflection. These assumptions are acknowledged, but they are central enough that broader stress tests under indoor, multi-light, soft-shadow, and low-light cases are needed.

The downstream shadow-removal study is suggestive but limited: it uses a small preference study rather than objective shadow-free ground truth, and the setup does not isolate whether gains come from truly accurate attached-shadow detection versus object-region post-processing.

Reproducibility details are incomplete in the manuscript text: the project page appears blank, and it is unclear whether the dataset, manual correction protocol, annotations, training code, and baseline retraining scripts will be released in a form sufficient to reproduce the reported numbers.

strengths: The paper addresses a meaningful and relatively underexplored problem: separating cast and attached shadows rather than predicting a single shadow mask. This is a well-motivated distinction for scene understanding and downstream shadow removal, and the manuscript makes a convincing case that attached shadows require geometry- and light-aware reasoning rather than only appearance-based segmentation.

The proposed iterative coupling between shadow segmentation and light-direction estimation is technically sensible and aligned with the physics of attached shadow formation. The use of surface normals and a light-derived partial attached-shadow map is simple, interpretable, and supported by ablations showing substantial gains over variants without normals or without iterative feedback.

The new dataset with explicit cast, attached, and undefined shadow annotations is a valuable contribution. Although built from existing datasets, the manual correction and standardized split/evaluation protocol provide a useful benchmark for a task that current datasets do not cleanly support.

Experiments are reasonably comprehensive: the paper compares with several shadow detection baselines, includes fine-tuned baselines, reports full/cast/attached metrics, provides ablations for geometry, iterations, and losses, and includes qualitative cross-dataset and shadow-removal application evidence.

The empirical gains for attached shadows are large: attached BER improves from the strongest fine-tuned baseline around 19.49 to 12.93, while full-shadow and cast-shadow performance remains competitive. This supports the main claim that explicit cast/attached modeling is useful.
weaknesses: The light-direction supervision is partly heuristic for SOBA and CUHK, derived from object-shadow centroids and depth estimates. This creates some circularity: the method is trained to predict pseudo-light labels derived from the same annotations and monocular geometry cues it later exploits. The paper acknowledges limitations but does not fully quantify how noisy or biased these pseudo-labels are outside the small calibrated WSRD subset.

The dataset is useful but still modest in scale and partially constrained: only 1,458 images, foreground-object-centered cast/attached labels, and undefined regions excluded from cast/attached evaluation. This limits how broadly the reported cast/attached metrics reflect dense whole-scene shadow understanding.

Baseline fairness could be stronger. Most prior methods are binary shadow detectors fine-tuned with full-shadow supervision, whereas the proposed model receives explicit cast/attached labels and geometry inputs. The paper includes a no-normal variant, but it would be more convincing to compare against stronger multiclass segmentation baselines trained with the same cast/attached labels, and against baselines augmented with the same normal-map input.

The method depends heavily on off-the-shelf monocular depth/normal estimation. Errors in normals directly affect predictions, and the paper shows this as a limitation, but the evaluation does not isolate robustness across different normal estimators or under depth failures.

The illumination model assumes a single dominant directional light, which is reasonable for many outdoor images but less appropriate for indoor, multi-source, soft-shadow, night, or indirect-light settings. This narrows the likely deployment scope relative to general shadow detection claims.

The shadow removal application is suggestive but relatively weak evidence: it relies on a preference study rather than quantitative shadow-free ground truth, and the comparison is between joint-mask and separate-mask guidance rather than a broader downstream evaluation.
